passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new cognitive training program on working memory in adults aged 50-65. The study recruited 120 participants and randomly assigned them to one of three groups: (1) training group, (2) active control group (engaged in general reading), and (3) passive control group (no intervention). Over a 12-week period, participants completed a battery of working memory tasks at baseline, mid-intervention, and post-intervention. The training group received 30‑minute sessions twice weekly that incorporated adaptive n‑back exercises. The active control group received 30‑minute sessions of non‑adaptive reading comprehension tasks. The passive control group received no sessions. Table 1 summarizes the mean scores (out of 100) and standard deviations for the primary working memory composite at post‑intervention. The researchers hypothesize that the training group will show a statistically significant improvement over both control groups. They plan to use a two‑way ANOVA to analyze group and time effects, followed by post‑hoc pairwise comparisons. The study also examines potential moderators such as baseline cognitive status and sleep quality.
stem: Which group achieved the highest mean working memory composite score at post-intervention?

options.D: Active Control and Passive Control tied

explanation: Correct: The training group mean was 78.5, above 72.3 and 70.1. Why the others are wrong: B) The active control mean was 72.3, below 78.5. C) The passive control mean was 70.1, the lowest. D) The two control means (72.3 and 70.1) differ and both are below training.
trap: Assuming the active control engaged in reading outscored the training group.

stem: Which experimental design element best supports the causal inference that the training program improves working memory?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to groups

explanation: Random assignment controls for confounding variables, allowing causal inference about the training program’s effect.
trap: Assuming the 12‑week duration alone establishes causality would be a trap.

stem: Assuming equal sample sizes, calculate the approximate effect size (Cohen’s d) between the training and passive control groups.
explanation: Pooled SD ≈ 8.66; difference in means = 8.4; d = 8.4 / 8.66 ≈ 0.97.
trap: Choosing 1.2 would overestimate the effect size.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The training group had the highest mean composite score.
options.B: The active control group's mean exceeded the passive control group's mean.
options.C: The training group's mean was 6.2 points above the active control group's mean.
options.D: The differences among the groups were statistically significant.

explanation: Correct: Table 1 gives only means and SDs; no test statistic or p-value is reported, and the passage says the researchers hypothesize significance and plan an ANOVA, so significance is not established. Why the others are wrong: A) the training mean (78.5) is the highest of 78.5, 72.3 and 70.1. B) the active control mean (72.3) exceeds the passive control mean (70.1). C) 78.5 − 72.3 = 6.2 points.
trap: Reading higher mean scores as established statistical significance when no test results are reported.

explanation: Examining moderators involves testing for interaction effects between group and baseline status.
trap: Assuming a main effect would ignore the moderator relationship.
